questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose to study at McGill in Montreal, Canada for several reasons: I wanted to explore Canada and Canadian culture, I wanted to improve my French and English (the two primary languages spoken in Montreal), and I wanted to attend a good university.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. McGill's website is very user friendly, and you can find all the information you need there: on how to apply to McGill, how to register for courses, what orientation events they offer etc. They also had a series of webinars on how to find housing and other practical stuff outside of the university.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn't receive any, because I didn't look for assistance. But I know McGill offers a lot of different services such as International Students Services, mental health services etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Unfortunately, I missed the orientation week, but I've heard it's a good opportunity to meet other students. There are also opportunities throughout the semester to meet other students. For example, I went on a hiking trip which I found through McGill's B2 Gym.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy. There were lots of apartments for rent. I looked for an apartment with four other people, and we managed to find a 5 bedroom apartment about 2 months in advance.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: In general, there is great public transport in Montreal, and also fairly good bicycle lanes, so even if you live off campus, it should still be manageable to get to school.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't choose any of the housing offered to students, but there is a lot of housing available in general.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't find it challenging, but it was a little time consuming.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: There are some different documents you need to upload such as letter of nomination, proof of English proficiency, university transcript etc. But it was manageable to get those documents, and I didn't even need to write a motivational letter.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I am not sure, I did not receive any help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not very succesful. I was unable to register for a lot of the classes I had planned because the spots were already filled by the time I was able to register (and I tried to register as soon as it was possible for exchange students). However, I still ended up with very interesting courses, and there is also an add/drop period during the first two weeks of the semester, where a spot might open for you in the classes you wanted (but you can't be sure of it)

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make a long list of courses you find interesting, and look into which of those courses fit together in a week/which courses don't overlap. You can for example use McGill's Visual Schedule Builder. It's nice to note down a few different course combinations, as all courses probably won't be available to you (e.g. if the class is already full when you try to register).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, I was very satisfied. I think my professors were engaged and approachable. I thought the quality of their teaching was in general good, the syllabuses were interesting, and the expectations to the students were fair (it was possible to obtain good grades as long as you showed up for the lectures).

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I only took 300-level courses - none of them were really challenging, but I still learned a lot.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I mostly took classes with a lot of students (+100), so it was mostly lectures where the professor talked most of the time, but students were also encouraged to ask questions.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: ANTH 338 Indigenous Studies of Anthropology; FRSL 212 Oral and Written French 1; GSFS 304 Postcolonial Feminist Theories; SOCI 333 Social Stratification; SOCI 370 Gender and Development.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Definitely ANTH 338 and a French class (if it's in your interest to learn French). 

ANTH 338 was about Indigeneity and Indigenous peoples, and focused a lot on settler colonialism as well as Indigenous ways of thinking and being in the world (it was almost a bit philosophical). The professor did not allow computers in class, but I thought it was really nice, and there were only assignments in the class (no in person exams), so you did not have to remember everything said in class.

I also took a French course just for fun (I couldn't get it transferred to KU). It was a very effective way to learn French (but expect a lot of homework that you have to hand in for every class!)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: My flight tickets were cancelled due to a strike, and I did not receive any refund. I had to buy new plane tickets that were very expensive at the time (about 8,500 DKK for a one way ticket).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: In general, I think grocery shopping is a bit cheaper than in Denmark (but only a little). Go to Dollarama where you can get inexpensive dry goods.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was satisfied with the opportunities, but didn't end up signing up for a lot.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I know they have different communities (religious, LGBTQ+ etc). There is also McGill's B2 Gym that offers a great variety of sports classes. At the beginning of the semester, they have orientation week where you can meet other students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I went on a hiking trip I found through the B2 gym - that was a fun way to meet other students!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel around Canada - there is so much beautiful nature to explore! I really enjoyed my trip to Banff and Jasper National Park (which is very far from Montreal, but really worth the travel), and I also enjoyed visiting Quebec City during Christmas.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy - as long as you're open to meet new people, it should be no problem.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: They speak more French than I expected in Montreal (which is a good thing, if you, like me, are trying to learn French) - though their French is quite different from European French, so it can be quite difficult to understand.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Their oppenness. Sometimes (especially at university) you have to approach people yourself, but my experience was that if you did so, they were very friendly and willing to talk.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) Try to approach people - many people want to connect, but won't always initiate themselves, 2) Pack for all different kinds of weather (it rains and snows/gets really cold, but is also warm in the summertime), 3) Once you've found some people you like, invite them out for coffee or to explore the city together (take initiative).

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: McGill has so many opportunities to meet other students - explore them before you go, and sign up for events in advance.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people who became my friends during my stay - it was really nice to be able to connect with strangers, and in a very short time become close to them.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Figuring out how to prioritize school vs socializing and exploring the city/country. I did spend more time studying than expected, but I also found the classes really interesting!!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
